'''John Law''' (1745–1810) was an English mathematician and clergyman who began his career as a [[Fellow]] of [[Christ's College, Cambridge]], and went on to become chaplain to the [[Lord Lieutenant of Ireland]] and [[Church of Ireland]] bishop of [[Bishop of Clonfert and Kilmacduagh|Clonfert and Kilmacduagh]] (1782–1787), [[Bishop of Killala and Achonry|Killala and Achonry]] (1787–1795), and finally of [[Bishop of Elphin|Elphin]] (1795–1810).

He was a lifelong friend and correspondent of the philosopher [[William Paley]].

==Early life==
The son of [[Edmund Law]], later [[Bishop of Carlisle]], and Mary Christian, Law was born at [[Greystoke, Cumbria|Greystoke]] in [[Cumberland]], where his father was [[Rector (ecclesiastical)|rector]]. He was educated at [[Charterhouse School]] and [[Christ's College, Cambridge]], where in 1766 he graduated Bachelor of Arts with [[first-class honours]] in the [[Mathematical Tripos]] and was named as [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|second Wrangler]].<ref name=select>Enos Bronson, ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=lPQ0AAAAMAAJ&pg=PA281 Memoir of the Life and Character of Dr. John Law]'' in ''Select Reviews of Literature, and Spirit of Foreign Magazines'', Vol. 4 (1810), online at books.google.co.uk</ref> He proceeded [[Master of Arts (Oxbridge and Dublin)|Master of Arts]] in 1769.<ref>{{acad|id= LW762J|name=Law, John}}</ref>

==Career==
Law became a [[Fellow]] of Christ's and an [[Anglicanism|Anglican]] clergyman, and spent several years as a [[tutor]] and lecturer at Cambridge. In 1773 his father gave him his first [[benefice]]s, as [[vicar]] of [[Warkworth, Northumberland|Warkworth]], Northumberland, and as [[prebendary]] of [[Carlisle, Cumbria|Carlisle]].<ref name=select/> In 1777 he was collated [[Archdeacon of Carlisle]]. In April 1782, he went to Ireland as chaplain to the [[Lord Lieutenant of Ireland]], [[William Cavendish-Bentinck, 3rd Duke of Portland]], who had large estates in [[Cumberland]].<ref name=dnb/>

Law was quickly nominated as [[Bishop of Clonfert and Kilmacduagh]] on 26 July 1782 and consecrated on 21 September. The same year, he graduated [[Doctor of Divinity]].<ref name=dnb/> The appointment to Clonfert was unexpected. It was later reported that the Duke of Portland, after a long legal battle with [[James Lowther, 1st Earl of Lonsdale|Sir James Lowther]] over estates in Carlisle, was anxious to reward a man who had helped him in that matter with other preferments then held by Law.<ref name=select/>

Law was a lifelong friend of [[William Paley]], with whom he corresponded for decades.<ref name=paley>[[William Paley]], Matthew Eddy, David M. Knight, ''Natural Theology: or, evidence of the existence and attributes of the Deity'', [https://books.google.com/books?id=3Biv-3XGZwwC&pg=PA328 p. 328] online at books.google.co.uk</ref> Paley and Law had been friends at Cambridge, where Law lectured on mathematics and Paley on [[metaphysics]] and [[ethics|morals]]. When Law became Bishop of Clonfert, Paley was his successor as Archdeacon of Carlisle, and it was the urging of Law which led Paley to expand his Cambridge lectures into his book ''The Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy'' (1785).<ref>{{cite EB1911|wstitle= Paley, William |volume= 20 | pages = 628&ndash;629  |quote= At the suggestion of his friend John Law (son of Edward Law, bishop of Carlisle...), Paley published (1785) his lectures, revised and enlarged, under the title of The Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy. The book at once became....}}</ref><ref>[[William Cowper]], ed. Thomas Wright, ''The Correspondence of William Cowper: arranged in chronological order'' Volume 2 (1904), [https://books.google.com/books?id=AholAAAAMAAJ&q=Clonfert p. 66] online at books.google.co.uk (snippet)</ref> In that work, the chapter on ''Reverencing the Deity'' was ascribed to Law.<ref name=select/> Among other matters, they corresponded on the scientific proofs which could be used to support a theological argument. In 1797, for instance, Law wrote to Paley: "In your chapter on divine contrivance, you must have an article on the [[Solar System|solar system]]..."<ref name=paley/>

On taking up the post in Clonfert, Law hired the mathematician [[John Howard (mathematician)|John Howard]] as his [[Steward (office)|steward]], but dispensed with Howard's services in 1786 after "an unfortunate marriage".<ref>R. E. Anderson, rev. Ruth Wallis, 'Howard, John (1753–1799)', in [[Oxford Dictionary of National Biography]] (Oxford University Press, 2004) [http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/13923, online version], accessed 11 May 2010</ref>

Law was translated to [[Bishop of Killala and Achonry|Killala and Achonry]] on 10 November 1787.<ref name=dnb>{{cite DNB|wstitle= Law, John (1745-1810) |volume= 32 |last= Reynell |first= W.A.|author-link= |pages= 234-235 |year= |short=1}}</ref> On learning that almost the whole population of his new see were [[Roman Catholic]]s, he commented: "That as it was a hopeless task to make them [[protestants]], it would answer every desirable purpose to make them ''good catholicks''." At his own expense, Law then distributed throughout the diocese a new edition of the Rev. John Gother's ''The Sincere Christian's Guide in the Choice of Religion''.<ref name=select/>

He was translated again to become [[Bishop of Elphin]] in 1795, being nominated on 11 March and appointed by [[letters patent]] on 27 March. He died in [[Dublin]] on 18 March 1810 and was buried in the Chapel of [[Trinity College, Dublin]], where he had founded prizes for mathematics.<ref name=dnb/>

==Family==
On 17 January 1782, while living in Carlisle, Law married Anne Thomlinson, a daughter of the Rev. William Plaskett and widow of John Thomlinson of [[Blencogo]], [[Cumberland]], but they had no children.<ref name=select/><ref name=dnb/><ref>Society of Antiquaries of Newcastle upon Tyne, ''Archaeologia aeliana, or, Miscellaneous tracts relating to antiquity'' (1885), [https://books.google.com/books?id=RowbAQAAIAAJ&q=%22John+Law%22+bishop p. 62] (snippet) online</ref> His wife, born on 4 August 1741, was the half-sister of [[James Wallace (British politician)|James Wallace]], [[barrister]], of [[Featherstone Castle]], Member of Parliament, [[Solicitor General for England and Wales|Solicitor General]] and [[Attorney General for England and Wales|Attorney General]], and the aunt of [[Thomas Wallace, 1st Baron Wallace]].<ref>[[John Burke (genealogist)|John Burke]], ''Burke's Genealogical and Heraldic History of the Landed Gentry'', Volume 2, [https://books.google.com/books?id=0NEKAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA1495 p. 1495] online at books.google.co.uk</ref>

Law was the elder brother of [[Ewan Law]] {{post-nominals|country=GBR|MP}} (1747–1829), of [[Edward Law, 1st Baron Ellenborough]] (1750–1818), who became [[Lord Chief Justice of England and Wales]], and of [[George Henry Law]] (1761–1845), [[Bishop of Chester]] and [[Bishop of Bath and Wells]].<ref name=dnb/> Another brother, [[Thomas Law (1756–1834)|Thomas Law]] (1756–1834), was a business man who settled first in [[British India]] and then in 1793 in the United States, where he married as his second wife [[Elizabeth Parke Custis Law|Eliza Parke Custis]], a granddaughter of [[Martha Washington]].<ref>Allen C. Clark, ''Thomas Law: A Biographical Sketch'' (Washington, D.C.: Press of W. F. Roberts, 1900), pp. 11–12: "Early in 1796 the engagement with Eliza Park Custis was announced... Thomas Law, youngest son of the late Bishop of Carlisle, to Miss Custis."</ref><ref>[[Thomas Jefferson]], ed. [[J. Jefferson Looney]], ''The Papers of Thomas Jefferson, Retirement Series'' (vol. 3, 2006), p. 209</ref> Eliza and Thomas Law divorced in 1811.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://gwpapers.virginia.edu/documents/marriage/bcustis2.html |title=The Papers of George Washington: Documents |publisher=The Papers of George Washington |work=gwpapers.virginia.edu |access-date=21 May 2010 |year=2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070829232620/http://gwpapers.virginia.edu/documents/marriage/bcustis2.html |archive-date=29 August 2007 }}</ref>

==Publications==
*''A Sermon preached at the Visitation of the Right Reverend the Lord Bishop of London: in the church of Thaxted, in Essex, on Wednesday, 28 May 1778'' (1778)<ref>John Law, ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=wQmnPwAACAAJ A sermon preached at the visitation of the Right Reverend the Lord Bishop of London]'' – details online at books.google.co.uk</ref>
*''Sermon preached in [[Christ Church Cathedral, Dublin|Christ Church, Dublin]], before the Incorporated Society'' (1796)
*''Sermon preached in [[St Paul's Cathedral|St Paul's Cathedral, London]], at the meeting of the [[charity school]] children'' (1797)
